title: Qualification criteria and the RFQ
objectives: Explain why qualification sets a minimum bar and why more competition is not always better competition
Choose between an open tender, pre-qualification and short listing for a given project
Describe the contents of an RFQ and the three categories of qualification criteria
Set sound financial and technical criteria, including net worth, experience and contractor equity rules
Apply good practice on short listing and consortium changes

sections.heading: 1. The purpose of qualification: a balanced bar
sections.body:
In the previous lesson, qualification appeared as one task of the Structuring Phase. Now we go deeper.

**Qualification** sets a **minimum bar of capability** for the bidder, whether a single company or a **bidding consortium**, that will enter the PPP contract. The aim is to reduce the risk of project failure caused by lack of capability and capacity.

Setting the bar is a balancing act:
- **Too high** a bar limits competition too much.
- **Too low** a bar may **discourage highly qualified bidders**, because they think they have a very low chance of winning.
- **More competition is not necessarily better competition.** With many qualified bidders, each has a lower chance of winning, so each is less willing to spend money on a good bid. Winners must also recover the costs of more lost bids.

So every project should **customise** its qualification levels to its own needs. In two-stage processes, where the legal framework allows, the criteria should aim for an **optimal number** of pre-qualified bidders rather than a large number.

By setting qualification requirements, the authority is **shaping the profile of its future private partner**. That partner will be with the government for decades, so qualification must cover every function it will perform: investment, raising finance, construction, operation and maintenance, and life-cycle management.

sections.heading: 2. Three qualification approaches
sections.body:
| Approach | How it works | When it fits |
|---|---|---|
| **Open tender** (one stage) | Qualifications submitted with the proposal; qualification checked first as pass/fail, then proposals evaluated | Government knows exactly what it wants; project not too complex in finance or technology |
| **Pre-qualification** | An RFQ stage first; everyone who passes the bar receives the RFP | Complex or large projects with a risk of few bids; authority wants to test market appetite |
| **Short listing** | Pre-qualified bidders are ranked; only the top few receive the RFP | Required for competitive dialogue and most negotiated processes; highly complex projects; retaining top bidders' interest |

**Open tender - pros:** shorter process; easy to handle (pass/fail only); lower costs for both sides; in theory more competition, but no more than pre-qualification. **Cons:** higher risk of protests from losing bidders; uncertainty about the number of rivals may discourage strong bidders; heavy pricing pressure may attract **reckless bidders** and discourage quality. Even the short timeline can be a danger.

**Pre-qualification - pros:** more time to prepare the RFP; no harder than qualification in an open tender; low cost for bidders; a **real test of market appetite** before the RFP, so the authority can react if responses are few; time to correct formal and non-material errors; bidders invest more in proposals once they know they are qualified; the authority knows who the real bidders are; lower risk of protest. **Cons:** longer process; if many bidders are qualified, strong ones may be discouraged, and pricing pressure may grow.

**Short listing - pros:** more time for the RFP; bidders invest even more when facing only a few rivals; better handling of large programmes; **lowest risk of protest**. **Cons:** competition may drop if short-listed bidders withdraw or do not submit an offer; a longer tender process and a longer time to sign the contract; higher costs for both sides in dialogue or interactive processes; more complex, because it needs evaluation and selection.

The Guide's rule of thumb: **the more complex and large the project, the more appropriate pre-qualification is.** Which approach is right also depends on the **maturity of the market**. Whatever the approach, qualification should always be done **before the bids are opened**.

sections.heading: 3. The RFQ and the three categories of criteria
sections.body:
The **Request for Qualifications (RFQ)**, called an **Invitation for Expressions of Interest (EOI)** in some countries, contains:
- the qualification criteria (or selection criteria for short listing);
- the requirements for the **Submission of Qualifications (SoQ)**: deadline, formats, documents and the evidence required, especially for experience;
- rules on **conflict of interest**, incompatibilities and **changes in consortium composition**;
- a summary of the project and the future contract structure.

Good practice is for governments to **standardise** the structure and form of the RFQ through PPP guidelines, including the evidence required. But pass/fail thresholds and short-listing criteria must always be **tailor-made** for the project. For complex or unique projects, the authority may use external consultants to draft the criteria.

There are three categories of criteria:
1. **Administrative or legal**: always **pass/fail**.
2. **Financial-economic capacity**.
3. **Technical capability or experience**.

Only categories 2 and 3 are used to **rank** bidders for a short list.

The Guide also asks procuring authorities to make sure the RFP requires designs that comply with climate provisions in national or international codes, and to include **climate KPIs** in the technical specifications, so performance is measurable across the life cycle. Where possible, the project should meet sustainability rating frameworks such as LEED, EDGE and SuRe, which also helps attract climate finance. Tender documents may separate sustainability, climate resilience, innovation, excellence and inclusivity criteria (for example, gender action plans).

sections.heading: 4. Legal qualification
sections.body:
Legal qualification checks the **formal regularity** of the bidder, especially its legal personality. Typical documents:
- evidence that each bidder (and each consortium member) **exists and is in good standing**;
- evidence of the **consortium agreement** and members' commitment;
- evidence of the **power of representatives** to act for each member;
- for foreign companies, a **registration or licence** to operate where required.

Bidders must also show they are up to date with **tax and labour** obligations by the proposal submission date.

Common rules:
- A bidder may **not join more than one consortium** (nor may its parent or subsidiaries).
- A company with a **vested interest**, such as an adviser to the procuring authority on the same process, cannot bid.

**Bad practice:** requiring bidders to create the **special purpose vehicle (SPV)** already at this stage. It is expensive and time-consuming for bidders.

Legal qualification is mainly a local legal matter, but the government must avoid creating **barriers for international bidders**.

sections.heading: 5. Financial-economic capacity
sections.body:
These criteria show that the bidder is financially healthy and able to meet the project's financial needs: **funds for equity** and the capacity to **raise long-term debt**.

**Net worth** is the most common criterion. Net worth = **assets minus liabilities**. It is usually sized to be **at least equal to the estimated equity investment** for the project, based on a gearing ratio.

**Aggregation.** Adding up net worth across several sponsors should be **not allowed or limited**. The government wants one member that can invest the required equity **on its own**. This member is usually the **Lead Member** and holds the **largest equity stake**, its skin in the game.

Other indicators: debt-to-equity or leverage, liquidity ratios, project ratios such as equity to project CAPEX, and average revenues or profits over the **last three years**. These are calculated from recent financial statements, normally no more than three years.

Good practices:
- Provide **specific forms** for financial data, with clearly defined ratios.
- Make criteria **as objective as possible**, with clear thresholds and calculation rules.
- Do not confuse financial capacity with **experience in raising project finance**. That experience belongs under **technical capability or experience** criteria.
- Bank **support letters** or **letters of comfort** are generally good practice, but their value as proof of solvency is limited. They should **not replace an active analysis** of the bidder's capacity.

International bidders may report under IFRS while local rules differ, which can make fair comparison difficult.

sections.heading: 6. Technical capacity and experience
sections.body:
Many projects fail because the winner lacks the skills for the project's challenges, or lacks experience in **one** of the required areas. For example, an experienced contractor with no experience or appetite to run the asset for decades or act as a long-term investor is a high risk. The Guide cites the **Channel Tunnel Rail Link** as a project that went wrong largely because the right skills were not required.

Experience should be shown on several fronts:
- **Construction** of similar projects (same sector, similar size and complexity);
- **Operation and maintenance** of similar infrastructure;
- **PPP management, investment and financial close** on similar projects;
- **Environmental and social**: minimum ESG standards or relevant sustainability experience.

Ongoing projects can count if **materially advanced**, for example construction at least 50 percent complete, or operations past the first two years.

**Must contractors be investors?** Generally the SPV owner need not be a contractor. The bidder can rely on a **named contractor** who is not a shareholder, with evidence of its commitment. Some jurisdictions only count contractors that take a minimum equity stake.

| | Require contractors to invest equity | Do not require it |
|---|---|---|
| Pros | Contractor has skin in the game; builds local PPP investment capability | Contractors without investment appetite can join; avoids conflicting roles; developers can bid without co-investing with contractors |
| Cons | May deter contractors; conflicting roles (equity seen as the price of buying the construction contract); may deter developers | No skin in the game for the contractor; may slow local industry development |

If required, set the stake prudently; **15 to 30 percent** is commonly seen. Leave enough room for contractors to team up with experienced PPP developers. In emerging markets where local contractors lack PPP experience, limiting the equity required from contractors makes joint ventures with specialist investors easier and helps build a national PPP industry.

**Typical indicators:** revenue in the relevant business; total CAPEX or number of projects built; total debt raised; number of qualifying similar projects above a minimum size; aggregated users or population served.

**Good practices:**
- Match criteria to the **partner profile** wanted.
- Allow **enough time** for SoQ; forming consortia takes time.
- Avoid **tailor-made requirements** that very few firms can meet. If only a few firms have a needed technology, consider short listing, letting the technology firm join **several consortia** as nominee, or selecting the supplier **separately**.
- Check that thresholds are **realistic**, using precedents, expert advice and market sounding.
- Define what counts as experience (active role, not passive investor), how **recent** it must be, and how it will be **verified** (client certificates or contacts).
- Avoid **double counting**, but note that aggregate volume and number of projects measure different things.
- Use **significance thresholds**, such as counting a project only if the member held a minimum equity share.
- Provide **templates** and keep **qualitative judgment** to a minimum.
- If bidders must describe how they see the project (for example, its key risks), say clearly when an answer counts as **unresponsive**: only when it shows a clear lack of interest and no useful information.

sections.heading: 7. Short listing and consortium changes
sections.body:
In **short listing**, pre-qualified bidders are **ranked** on their responses, and only the highest-ranked go to the RFP stage. It is generally necessary in two-stage processes with a **dialogue or interaction** phase. The usual number is **three to five** (the state of Victoria, Australia, may short list only two).

If the number that pass the pass/fail test equals the target number, no ranking is needed. Otherwise:
- The RFQ must explain the **evaluation criteria, their weightings and how each is scored**.
- Qualitative assessment is uncommon, though some sub-criteria need judgment, for example how similar an experience is.
- Scoring can attract concerns about subjectivity. If only a minimum score adds value, a pass/fail test can be used instead.
- Profile the **most suitable private partner** before choosing weightings, because weightings decide who is on the list.

**Consortium changes.** The RFQ should say whether changes are allowed after selection:
- Replacing or removing members should generally **not** be allowed, except in exceptional cases such as a member's **bankruptcy**.
- Some jurisdictions allow **new members** to join if they had no role in another short-listed consortium and existing members keep their roles.
- Flexibility, **provided the lead members do not change**, can help when the full skill mix is only clear once the RFP is seen.

**Key points (Box 5.22):** qualification rules should allow the experience of any consortium member to count if it commits equity or a specific role; allow consortia, especially so less experienced local firms in emerging markets can join experienced partners; and rely on **clarity, objectivity and transparency**.

example.title: Eastport Metro Line: setting the qualification bar
example.body:
Imagine the fictional city of Eastport preparing a large, complex metro PPP using competitive dialogue. Estimated equity is 200 million.

1. **Approach.** Because the project is complex and uses dialogue, the city runs pre-qualification with **short listing** of four bidders.
2. **Legal.** Pass/fail: good standing, consortium agreement, powers of representatives, tax and labour compliance. No firm may join two consortia. The city does **not** require an SPV at this stage.
3. **Financial.** The Lead Member must have net worth of at least 200 million **on its own**, and hold the largest equity stake. Bank letters of comfort are requested but the city still analyses the financial statements.
4. **Technical.** Construction, O&M and PPP financial-close experience on similar metro projects; construction references must be at least 50 percent complete.
5. **Technology problem.** Only two firms supply the required signalling system. Instead of a tailor-made rule that only two consortia could meet, the city lets these suppliers join several consortia as nominee subcontractors.
6. **Ranking.** The RFQ publishes the scoring and weightings for financial and technical criteria only.

Six consortia apply, five pass, and the top four are short listed.

examTraps.trap: Assuming more qualified bidders always means better competition
examTraps.fix: Many qualified bidders lower each one's chance of winning, so they spend less on bids and strong firms may walk away. Aim for an optimal number, not a large one.

examTraps.trap: Ranking bidders for a short list on legal criteria
examTraps.fix: Administrative or legal criteria are always pass/fail. Only financial-economic and technical criteria are used to rank and select a short list.

examTraps.trap: Treating experience in raising project finance as financial capacity
examTraps.fix: Financial capacity means funds for equity and ability to raise debt, shown by net worth and ratios. Experience in raising project finance belongs under technical capability or experience.

examTraps.trap: Letting consortium members add up their net worth freely
examTraps.fix: Aggregation should be disallowed or limited, so one member, usually the Lead Member, can fund the required equity on its own.

examTraps.trap: Mixing up pre-qualification and short listing
examTraps.fix: Pre-qualification lets everyone who passes the bar receive the RFP. Short listing ranks the pre-qualified bidders and only the top few, usually three to five, receive it.

keyTerms.meaning: A condition a party must meet to have the right to bid, setting a minimum bar of capability.
The document setting qualification criteria and the rules and evidence for the Submission of Qualifications.
A qualification stage held before the RFP; all bidders who pass the bar receive the RFP.
Ranking pre-qualified bidders and inviting only a limited number, usually three to five, to the RFP stage.
Assets minus liabilities; usually required to be at least equal to the project's estimated equity.
The consortium member that can invest the required equity on its own and holds the largest equity stake.
The bidder's response to the RFQ, with the required documents and evidence.
A bank support letter on a bidder's capacity to raise funds; useful but of limited value as proof.
A rule that a past project counts as experience only if the consortium member held more than a minimum share of the equity in it.

summary: Qualification sets a minimum bar of capability; too high limits competition, too low deters strong bidders.
More competition is not necessarily better competition; aim for an optimal number of qualified bidders.
Open tender suits simple, clear projects; pre-qualification suits large and complex ones; short listing is used with dialogue.
Three criteria: legal (always pass/fail), financial-economic and technical; only the last two rank a short list.
Net worth should at least equal expected equity, held by one Lead Member; letters of comfort do not replace analysis.
Technical criteria must cover construction, O&M and PPP investment; avoid tailor-made, unrealistic or unverifiable rules.
Short lists are usually three to five; publish weightings and generally forbid consortium changes except in exceptional cases.

slides.title: Why qualify bidders?
points: Set a minimum bar of capability
slides.narration: In this lesson we look at qualification. Before anyone can bid, the authority checks that they are capable enough. Why? Because a PPP partner will be with you for decades. If it lacks money, skills or experience in any function, the project can fail. So qualification sets a minimum bar. And here is a nice way to think about it: when you write the qualification rules, you are really drawing a picture of the partner you want. Choose that picture carefully.

slides.title: Setting the bar
slides.narration: Setting the bar is a balance. If it is too high, too few firms can compete. If it is too low, strong firms may stay away, because they see many weak rivals and a small chance of winning. The Guide stresses that more competition is not necessarily better competition. With many bidders, each spends less on its proposal, and the winners must recover the cost of more lost bids. So in two-stage processes, aim for an optimal number of qualified bidders, not the biggest number.

slides.title: Three approaches
points: Open tender: pass/fail with the bid
Short listing: rank and select a few
slides.narration: There are three ways to qualify. In an open, one-stage tender, bidders send qualifications with their proposal, and qualification is a pass or fail check. It is quick and cheap, but best when the project is simple. In pre-qualification, there is an RFQ stage first, and everyone who passes gets the RFP. This suits large and complex projects and tests market appetite early. In short listing, pre-qualified bidders are ranked and only the top few go forward. It is always used with competitive dialogue.

slides.title: The RFQ and three criteria
slides.narration: The RFQ sets out the criteria, the deadline, the documents and forms, the evidence required, and rules on conflicts of interest and consortium changes. There are three categories of criteria. Legal or administrative criteria are always pass or fail. Financial and technical criteria can also be pass or fail, but only these two are used to rank bidders for a short list. Standard templates help, but the actual thresholds must always be tailored to the specific project.

slides.title: Legal qualification
points: Do not require an SPV yet
slides.narration: Legal qualification checks that the bidder formally exists and can bid. It asks for proof of good standing, the consortium agreement, the powers of the people signing, licences for foreign firms, and tax and labour compliance. Usually, one company cannot join two consortia, and the authority's own advisers cannot bid. One common mistake is asking bidders to create their project company at this stage. The Guide calls that bad practice, because it is costly and slow. Also, avoid rules that block international bidders.

slides.title: Financial capacity
points: Net worth at least equal to equity
Letters of comfort are not enough
slides.narration: Financial criteria show the bidder can put in equity and raise debt. The main test is net worth, which is assets minus liabilities. It should be at least equal to the equity the project needs. And adding up net worth across members should be limited, so that one member, the Lead Member, can provide the equity alone. Other ratios, like leverage and liquidity, help too. Bank letters of comfort are welcome, but they do not replace a real analysis of the accounts.

slides.title: Technical experience
slides.narration: Technical experience is where many projects succeed or fail. A great builder with no interest in running the asset for thirty years is a real risk. So ask for experience in construction, operation and maintenance, and PPP investment and financial close. Be careful with the rules. Avoid requirements that only one or two firms can meet. If a special technology has few suppliers, let them join several consortia, or buy that technology separately. Define how recent experience must be, and how you will check it.

slides.title: Short listing in practice
slides.narration: Finally, short listing. It is normal with competitive dialogue, and the usual short list is three to five bidders. The RFQ must publish the criteria, their weightings and how each is scored, so the ranking is transparent. Decide the partner profile first, because the weightings decide who makes the list. Once selected, consortia should not normally swap or drop members, except in cases like bankruptcy. Some flexibility is possible if the lead members stay the same. Clarity, objectivity and transparency are the keys.

quiz.question: A procuring authority is preparing a large, complex hospital PPP and fears few bidders will respond. It wants to test market appetite before issuing the RFP. Which approach fits best?
options: An open one-stage tender with qualification submitted alongside proposals
Pre-qualification through a separate RFQ stage
Direct negotiation with the largest local contractor
Skipping qualification and evaluating price only
quiz.explanation: Pre-qualification allows a real test of market appetite before the RFP, so the authority can react if responses are few, and it suits large and complex projects. An open tender is best when the project is simple and clear.

quiz.question: An authority will use competitive dialogue for a complex rail PPP. Eight consortia pass the pass/fail test. What should the authority do?
options: Invite all eight to the dialogue, because more competition is always better
Select bidders by lottery to avoid subjectivity
Rank them on financial and technical criteria; short list three to five
Rank them using the legal criteria and choose the top two
quiz.explanation: Short listing is always used with dialogue processes, usually three to five, ranked by published financial and technical criteria. Legal criteria are always pass/fail and are not used for ranking.

quiz.question: A PPP's estimated equity requirement is 150 million. How should the authority design the net worth criterion?
options: At least 150 million of net worth held by one member, usually the Lead Member
Allow consortium members to add up their net worth freely to reach 150 million
Require net worth equal to the total project CAPEX
Accept bank letters of comfort instead of any net worth test
quiz.explanation: Net worth is usually sized at least equal to expected equity, and aggregation should be disallowed or limited so one member can fund the equity alone. Letters of comfort have limited value and should not replace analysis.

quiz.question: A draft RFQ requires each bidding consortium to incorporate its project company (SPV) before submitting qualifications. How does the Guide view this?
options: Good practice, because it proves the members' real commitment
Required by all PPP laws for consortium bids
Acceptable, but only for foreign bidders in the consortium
Generally bad practice, as it is costly and slow for bidders
quiz.explanation: The Guide says requiring an SPV at the qualification stage is generally regarded as bad practice because it imposes an unnecessary cost and delay. At this stage the Guide asks for evidence of the consortium agreement and the members' commitment instead.

quiz.question: A drafter proposes scoring bidders' experience in raising project finance under the financial-economic capacity criteria. What should the procuring authority do?
options: Accept it, since raising finance is a financial matter
Delete the criterion, since finance experience is irrelevant
Move it to the technical capability or experience criteria
Make it a legal pass/fail criterion
quiz.explanation: The Guide warns that experience in raising project finance is easily confused with financial capacity and is better handled under experience or technical capability. Financial capacity concerns funds for equity and capacity to raise debt.

quiz.question: A light rail project needs a signalling technology that only two companies in the world supply. How should the authority avoid limiting competition?
options: Require each consortium to own one of the two suppliers outright
Let the suppliers join several consortia as nominee contractors
Qualify only the two suppliers as bidders
Remove all technical criteria from the RFQ
quiz.explanation: The Guide suggests options such as letting the technology company join several consortia, running a short list, or selecting the supplier separately. Tailor-made requirements that few firms can meet reduce competition.

quiz.question: A government wants to require construction contractors to hold equity in bidding consortia. What is a risk the Guide highlights?
options: A contractor may see equity as the price of the works and neglect oversight
Contractors will always end up with too much skin in the game
Lenders will refuse to finance any consortium that includes a building contractor
It removes the need for any technical qualification of bidders
quiz.explanation: Requiring contractor equity can create conflicting roles: the contractor may see its equity as the price of the construction contract and not perform the oversight expected of an investor. It may also discourage contractors without investment appetite.

quiz.question: After short listing, one consortium wants to replace a member simply because it found a partner with a better price. There is no bankruptcy or similar event. What should normally happen?
options: Allow it, because consortia may change freely after short listing
Allow it only if the lead member is replaced
Disqualify all consortia and restart the RFQ
Refuse it; replacements are allowed only in exceptional cases
quiz.explanation: The Guide says replacing or removing members should generally not be allowed except in exceptional cases such as bankruptcy. Some flexibility may be allowed provided the lead members do not change, not the other way round.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a disadvantage of an open one-stage tender listed in the Guide?
options: Higher risk of protests from losing bidders
Uncertainty about the number of rivals may deter strong bidders
Pricing pressure may attract reckless bidders
Higher costs for bidders than in any other approach
quiz.explanation: Lower cost for bidders and the authority is actually listed as an advantage of the open tender. Protests, deterred strong bidders and reckless pricing are all listed disadvantages.

quiz.question: Consider two statements. 1: Administrative and legal qualification criteria are always pass/fail. 2: Qualification may be completed after bids are opened if the authority is short of time.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Legal criteria are always pass/fail. The Guide says pre-selection or qualification should always be done before the bids are opened, so statement 2 is false.

quiz.question: An authority sets very low qualification thresholds for a metro PPP so that almost any firm can bid. What risk does the Guide highlight?
options: Too few bidders will then be able to pass the qualification stage
Highly qualified firms may stay away, seeing little chance to win
Legal criteria will then have to be scored instead of pass/fail
The RFQ will become far too long for bidders to prepare
quiz.explanation: A bar set too low may discourage highly qualified bidders because they perceive a very low chance of winning (Ch 5 §7). Too few qualified bidders is the risk of a bar set too high.

quiz.question: Why may a large number of pre-qualified bidders in a two-stage process compromise outcomes?
options: The authority must then repay every losing bidder's bid costs
Lenders refuse to finance more than three bidders in any tender
Legal checks become impossible to complete before the deadline
Each bidder's chance falls, so it spends less on its proposal
quiz.explanation: With many bidders, each one's chance of success is lower, so bidders are less willing to spend funds on bidding (Ch 5 §7.3). The Guide does not say the authority repays bid costs.

quiz.question: Consider two statements. 1: With more bidders, winners must recover the costs of more lost bids. 2: In two-stage processes, criteria should aim for the largest possible number of pre-qualified bidders.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false: where the legal framework allows, criteria should give an optimal number of pre-qualified bidders rather than a large number (Ch 5 §7.3).

quiz.question: The Guide cites the Channel Tunnel Rail Link. What lesson does this case illustrate?
options: Success from short listing only two bidders in a dialogue
The danger of letting members add up their net worth
The value of marketing a project early to industry
Failure caused largely by not requiring the right skills
quiz.explanation: The Channel Tunnel Rail Link went wrong to a significant extent because the right skills and capacity were not required of bidders (Ch 5 §7.3). It is a technical qualification lesson.

quiz.question: A city wants a simple car park PPP. It knows exactly what it wants, and the finance and technology are not complex. Which qualification approach fits best?
options: An open one-stage tender with pass/fail qualification
Short listing of three bidders followed by competitive dialogue
Pre-qualification with a ranked short list of five bidders
A direct award to the largest local construction firm
quiz.explanation: Table 5.5 says governments should use the open tender only when it is very clear what they want and the project is not too complex in financing and technical terms (Ch 5 §7). Dialogue would add time and cost.

quiz.question: An RFQ asks bidders to show they are up to date with tax payments and labour laws. By when should this evidence be provided?
options: Only after the contract has been awarded
Within one year of financial close
By the proposal submission date
Only if a losing bidder files a protest
quiz.explanation: Tax and labour compliance is usually checked for each bidder, and the evidence should be provided by the proposal submission date (Ch 5 §7.1). Checking it after award would be too late to exclude a non-compliant bidder.

quiz.question: A bidder's qualification submission contains a formal, non-material error. Which approach gives the authority time to have it corrected before proposals are due?
options: Pre-qualification through a separate RFQ stage
An open one-stage tender with qualifications in the bid
A price-only tender with a single sealed envelope
A direct negotiation with the first bidder to apply
quiz.explanation: Table 5.5 lists as a benefit of pre-qualification that it allows time to correct formal and other non-material errors in the qualification submission (Ch 5 §7). In a one-stage tender, there is no separate stage to fix them.

quiz.question: Which of these is a disadvantage of pre-qualification with no short listing?
options: It costs bidders much more than an open one-stage tender does
It gives the authority no test of market appetite
Many pre-qualified bidders may discourage strong firms
It leaves no time to correct errors in submissions
quiz.explanation: If many bidders are pre-qualified, some strong bidders may see too much competition and be discouraged, and price pressure may grow (Table 5.5). Low bidder cost and a market test are advantages of pre-qualification.

quiz.question: An authority short lists four bidders for a dialogue process, and two of them withdraw before the RFP. Which disadvantage of short listing does this show?
options: Open tenders carry a higher risk of protests by losers
Competition may drop if short-listed bidders drop out
Pre-qualification makes the tender process longer
Legal criteria must always be applied as pass/fail
quiz.explanation: Table 5.5 lists as a con of short listing that competition may be reduced, especially if short-listed bidders abandon or do not submit an offer (Ch 5 §7).

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a disadvantage of short listing in the Guide?
options: A longer time to sign the contract
Less time to prepare the RFP
Higher costs in dialogue processes
More complex, as it needs evaluation
quiz.explanation: Short listing actually gives more time to prepare the RFP, which is an advantage (Table 5.5). Longer signature time, higher costs in dialogue and more complexity are listed disadvantages.

quiz.question: Consider two statements. 1: The right qualification approach depends partly on the maturity of the market. 2: Qualitative assessment is a common part of short-listing criteria.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Statement 1 is true (Box 5.22). Statement 2 is false: including qualitative assessment in short-listing criteria is uncommon, although some sub-criteria may involve some judgment, such as how similar an experience is (Ch 5 §7.4).

quiz.question: A national PPP unit wants to standardise its RFQs across all projects. What must remain tailor-made for each project?
options: The structure and general form of the RFQ document
The type of evidence required for financial data
The general list of legal documents to be submitted
The pass/fail thresholds and short-listing criteria
quiz.explanation: Standardising the RFQ structure, forms and evidence through PPP guidelines is good practice, but pass/fail thresholds and short-listing criteria must always be tailor-made (Box 5.22).

quiz.question: A procuring authority faces a unique and highly complex project and is unsure how to set the qualification criteria. What may it do?
options: Let each bidder propose its own qualification criteria
Copy another country's thresholds without any change
Use external consultants to help draft the criteria
Drop qualification and evaluate the bids on price only
quiz.explanation: The Guide notes that, due to complexity or uniqueness, the public sector might seek external consultants to draft qualification criteria (Ch 5 §7). Bidder-written criteria would not be neutral.

quiz.question: An authority wants the climate performance of a new hospital to be measurable over its whole life cycle. What does the Guide suggest?
options: Rely on bidders' general statements about climate policy
Check climate performance only at hand-back of the asset
Add climate performance to the legal pass/fail criteria
Include climate KPIs in the technical specifications
quiz.explanation: Climate KPIs should be included in the technical specifications to create measurable output expectations over the life cycle (Ch 5 §7). General statements are not measurable.

quiz.question: Which document is part of legal qualification?
options: An audited financial statement showing the member's net worth
A list of similar projects the member has built
A bank letter of comfort on raising funds
Evidence of the powers of each member's representatives
quiz.explanation: Legal qualification covers good standing, the consortium agreement, powers of representatives and licences for foreign firms (Ch 5 §7.1). Net worth and letters of comfort are financial; project lists are technical.

quiz.question: Company A leads one consortium. Its subsidiary wants to join a rival consortium in the same tender. What does common RFQ practice say?
options: Allowed, because the two are separate legal entities
Not allowed; related firms cannot join a rival consortium
Allowed, if the subsidiary holds under 15 percent equity
Allowed, but only when the subsidiary is a foreign company
quiz.explanation: It is general practice to prohibit a bidder, or any of its subsidiaries or parent companies, from participating in more than one consortium (Ch 5 §7.1).

quiz.question: The firm that advised the procuring authority on this same tender now wants to join a bidding consortium. What should happen?
options: It may bid if it discloses its earlier advice publicly
It should be barred, because it has a vested interest
It may bid, but with a price penalty added to its offer
It may bid if it is later short listed on merit alone
quiz.explanation: RFQs commonly prevent a company with a vested interest, such as an adviser to the procuring authority in the same process, from bidding (Ch 5 §7.1).

quiz.question: A draft RFQ requires every bidder to have been registered locally for five years before bidding. What concern does the Guide raise?
options: It is too weak to count as a real legal test
It conflicts with the net worth rule for lead members
It may create a barrier for international bidders
It should be scored rather than applied as pass/fail
quiz.explanation: Legal qualification is mainly a local matter, but the government must avoid creating barriers for international bidders (Ch 5 §7.1). Foreign firms should only need a registration or licence where the activity requires it.

quiz.question: What do financial-economic capacity criteria aim to show about a bidder?
options: Experience in operating and maintaining similar assets
Funds for equity and capacity to raise long-term debt
Good legal standing of each consortium member
Ability to design the project to the specifications
quiz.explanation: Financial capacity criteria show the bidder can meet the project's financial needs: funds for equity and capacity to raise third-party long-term debt (Ch 5 §7.2). Operating experience is a technical criterion.

quiz.question: A draft RFQ asks for ten years of financial statements to calculate financial ratios. What does the Guide suggest?
options: Keep all ten years, as this is the standard practice
Use recent statements, normally no more than three years
Use only forecast statements prepared for the project
Use the financial statements of the future project company
quiz.explanation: Indicators are calculated from the balance sheet and profit and loss of the previous year or a few recent years, normally no more than three (Ch 5 §7.2). The SPV does not yet exist at qualification.

quiz.question: A draft RFQ says financial capacity will be judged 'as the evaluation committee sees fit'. What should the authority change?
options: Nothing, since some judgment is always unavoidable
Replace the test with bank letters of comfort only
Set clear thresholds, defined ratios and specific forms
Move financial capacity into the legal pass/fail criteria
quiz.explanation: Financial criteria should be as objective as possible, with clear thresholds, defined ratios and forms showing how to calculate and present each indicator (Ch 5 §7.2).

quiz.question: A bidder with weak accounts submits a strongly worded bank letter of comfort. What should the authority do?
options: Accept the letter as full and final proof of solvency
Still analyse its capacity; the letter's value is limited
Reject the letter, because such letters are bad practice
Ask the bank that wrote the letter to join the consortium
quiz.explanation: Letters of comfort are generally good practice, but their value as proof of solvency is limited and should not substitute for an active analysis of the bidder's capacity (Ch 5 §7.2).

quiz.question: A world-class builder with no appetite to run the asset or act as a long-term investor bids alone for a 30-year PPP. How does the Guide view this?
options: Ideal, because construction is the biggest PPP risk of all
Acceptable, provided its net worth is high enough
A high risk of failure, since not all functions are covered
Acceptable, because operations are not assessed in PPPs
quiz.explanation: Failure can occur if the winner lacks experience in all areas of the contract cycle; an experienced contractor with no appetite to manage the asset or invest long term is a high risk (Ch 5 §7.3).

quiz.question: A consortium cites a similar hospital whose construction is only 30 percent complete as experience. Under a common rule in tenders, does it count?
options: No; many tenders need at least 50 percent completion
Yes; any ongoing project always counts as experience
Yes, as long as the bidder is the Lead Member
No; only projects operating for ten years can count
quiz.explanation: Ongoing projects often count if materially advanced; many tenders require construction to be at least 50 percent complete, or operations past the first two years (Ch 5 §7.3).

quiz.question: An investor-led consortium has no construction firm among its shareholders. How can it usually show construction experience?
options: It cannot qualify unless a contractor becomes a shareholder
Rely on a named contractor with evidence of its commitment
It can use the construction record of its lenders
It can promise to choose a contractor after the award
quiz.explanation: Generally the SPV owner need not be a contractor; the bidder can rely on a named contractor that is not a shareholder, with evidence of its commitment (Ch 5 §7.3). Some jurisdictions, however, only count contractors with equity.

quiz.question: A government decides that contractors in bidding consortia must also invest equity. What stake level does the Guide say is commonly seen?
options: Between 15 and 30 percent
Between 51 and 70 percent
The full 100 percent
Between 1 and 5 percent
quiz.explanation: If contractor equity is required, the level should be prudently assessed; 15 to 30 percent is commonly seen (Ch 5 §7.3). A majority stake would deter contractors and developers.

quiz.question: Which is an advantage of requiring contractors to also be equity investors?
options: It prevents conflicting contractor and investor roles
It lets contractors with no appetite to invest join bids
It gives the contractor a stake in overall project success
It helps developers who avoid co-investing with builders
quiz.explanation: Requiring contractor equity gives the contractor skin in the game (Table 5.6). The other three options are advantages of NOT requiring contractors to invest.

quiz.question: In an emerging market where local contractors lack PPP experience, how should an authority treat contractor equity in its RFQ?
options: Require local contractors to hold majority equity stakes
Exclude local contractors from all bidding consortia
Make each local contractor act as the Lead Member
Limit it, to ease joint ventures with specialist investors
quiz.explanation: In EMDE markets, limiting contractors' equity investment helps joint ventures between local contractors and specialist investors and builds a national PPP industry (Ch 5 §7.3).

quiz.question: An authority gives bidders two weeks to submit qualifications for a large, complex PPP. What is the concern?
options: Forming consortia takes significant time, so allow more
Two weeks is too long and will delay the tender launch
An SoQ is just as demanding as a full proposal
Submission time only matters in one-stage open tenders
quiz.explanation: Sufficient time is needed for the SoQ: although it is less demanding than a proposal, finding partners and agreeing consortium terms takes significant time (Ch 5 §7.3).

quiz.question: How should an authority check that its experience thresholds are realistic and achievable?
options: Set them at the level of the largest global firm
Ask each likely bidder in a private meeting
Copy the thresholds from the last tender exactly
Use precedents, expert advice and market sounding
quiz.explanation: The Guide says successful precedents help but need expert advice, and thresholds may be investigated through market sounding before qualification (Ch 5 §7.3). Private meetings would harm transparency.

quiz.question: An RFQ counts a past project as experience only if the consortium member held more than a minimum share of equity in it. What is this rule called?
options: A significance threshold
A gearing cap rule
An equity lock-in rule
An aggregation limit rule
quiz.explanation: Significance level thresholds count experience only where the member invested more than a set percentage of the equity, showing substantial involvement (Ch 5 §7.3). Gearing caps and lock-ins are contract terms.

quiz.question: How can an authority make sure the experience bidders claim can be validated?
options: Accept the bidder's own signed statement as sufficient proof
Rely on press articles written about the projects
Ask for client certificates or a client contact person
Use the bidder's marketing brochures and website
quiz.explanation: Evidence must be capable of validation, for example certificates from the government or client, or contact details of a key client person (Ch 5 §7.3).

quiz.question: An RFQ scores both the total passengers handled and the number of qualifying transport projects. A bidder complains this is double counting. How does the Guide view it?
options: It is real duplication, so one criterion must be removed
It is duplication, so both criteria must become pass/fail
Not necessarily duplication; each shows different experience
Double counting of experience is always acceptable in RFQs
quiz.explanation: Aggregated volume and number of qualifying projects are not necessarily duplication, because they show different forms of experience (Ch 5 §7.3). Real duplication should still be avoided.

quiz.question: An RFQ asks bidders to describe the project's key risks. When should a response be treated as unresponsive?
options: Whenever it differs from the authority's own view of the risks
Only when it shows clear lack of interest and no useful content
Whenever it is much shorter than the other bidders' responses
Whenever it lists fewer than ten key risks for the project
quiz.explanation: Good practice is to state clearly that a response is unresponsive only when there is a very clear lack of interest and complete absence of valuable information (Ch 5 §7.3).

quiz.question: Five consortia pass the pass/fail test, and the target short list is five. What evaluation is needed?
options: A ranking of the five on the legal criteria
A lottery to remove one of the consortia
A new RFQ to attract more candidates first
No ranking is needed; all five go forward
quiz.explanation: No evaluation is needed when the number of candidates passing the pass/fail test equals the number sought (Ch 5 §7.4). Ranking is only needed when there are more candidates than places.

quiz.question: An authority plans to short list bidders. What must its RFQ explain?
options: Only the names of the firms expected to apply
Only the legal documents that must be submitted
Nothing more, so that the panel keeps its full flexibility
The criteria, their weightings and how each is scored
quiz.explanation: Evaluation criteria must be clearly settled in the RFQ, including each criterion's weight in the overall score and how it will be scored (Ch 5 §7.4). Hidden weightings attract claims of subjectivity.

quiz.question: Why should an authority profile the most suitable private partner before deciding the short-listing weightings?
options: Because the partner profile replaces the RFQ
Because the weightings are always fixed by law
Because the weightings decide who makes the short list
Because the partner profile is needed to register the SPV
quiz.explanation: Care should be taken to profile the most suitable partner before deciding the weighting, as this will define which firms or consortia form the short list (Ch 5 §7.4).

quiz.question: A short-listed consortium wants to add a new member that had no role in any other short-listed consortium, while existing members keep their roles. What do some jurisdictions allow?
options: Always forbid any new member after selection
Allow the new member under those conditions
Allow it only if the lead member also leaves
Allow it only after the contract is signed
quiz.explanation: Some jurisdictions allow new members to join if they had no previous involvement in any short-listed consortium and existing members retain their roles (Ch 5 §7.4).

quiz.question: Consider two statements. 1: Flexibility on consortium changes can help when the full skill mix only becomes clear after bidders see the RFP. 2: This flexibility is acceptable even if the lead members change.
options: Only 1 is true
Only 2 is true
Both are true
Neither is true
quiz.explanation: Statement 1 is true. Statement 2 is false: the Guide supports flexibility provided that the lead members do not change (Ch 5 §7.4).

quiz.question: In an emerging market, a local firm with little PPP experience wants to bid. What should the qualification rules allow?
options: Only single firms bidding on their own, without any consortia
Local firms bidding alone, so their own skills are tested
Consortia with experienced partners, counting their experience
Only the Lead Member's experience counting toward the bar
quiz.explanation: Box 5.22 says rules should allow consortia, especially so less experienced firms in EMDE countries can join experienced partners, and count any member's experience if it commits equity or a specific role.
